metadata.title: The Test That Lied
metadata.purpose: Provenance Gatekeeper Development Log, Week 10 — a success message printed by code that never made the request, the GitHub Actions pipeline built to stop trusting manual testing, and the uncomfortable fact that CI would not have caught this particular bug either.

metadata.series_note: Week 7 (claude-gatekeeper-ci-pipeline, 'Unautomated Security') already built the pytest harness and the GitHub Actions pipeline. This reel is NOT that reel again: it is organised around the false positive named in the Week 10 hook — a webhook that reported success without ever sending a request — and it ends on the fact that a weak test passes that bug straight through a green pipeline. The runner and pytest beats are compressed to make room for it. The bug also retracts a claim made in Week 9 (claude-gatekeeper-n8n-incident); that retraction is stated out loud in B00.

beats.narration_text: Hi, I am Onkar Bhujbal. Last week I told you the Provenance Gatekeeper fired a webhook to our n8n server, and I showed you the terminal saying so. That was not true. I had written the success message and forgotten to write the HTTP request underneath it. The code printed a checkmark and did nothing. My manual testing watched it happen and agreed. So this week I am taking manual testing away from myself.

beats.narration_text: The bug was not the missing request. The bug was that something reported success without checking anything — and for a week, so did I. That is the failure worth fixing.

The code lied.

beats.authoring_note: Both readings are true sentences: 'The code lied.' and, corrected, 'The check lied.' — the correction moves the blame from the code to the verification, which is the reel's thesis.

beats.narration_text: Here is what the function looked like. It built the payload. It logged a checkmark. And then it returned. There is no request in it. Every human who read this function, including me, read the checkmark and stopped. The string said the thing had happened, so we believed the thing had happened.

beats.honesty_note: Reconstructed to the shape Onkar describes in the script — payload built, success printed, request absent. Not a verbatim paste of the shipped file.

beats.narration_text: So the fix is to stop being the one who checks. A workflow file now sits in the repository, and on every push to main, a clean Ubuntu machine in the cloud starts from nothing. It checks out the code, installs Python and the dependencies, and runs the Pytest suite against FastAPI's test client — including the adversarial payloads and the token authentication cases. None of it is on my laptop, and none of it waits for me.

beats.narration_text: If one test fails, or the container refuses to build because two dependencies disagree, the run goes red and the merge button stops working. That is the part that matters. Not the notification — the fact that I cannot click past it. The branch protection rule is the whole mechanism; without it a red pipeline is just a red icon next to a merge that happened anyway.

beats.honesty_note: neverArms is set because the beat narrates a BLOCKED merge. The script's visual asks for the green checkmark and the glowing Merge button; the reel shows the red case instead, because a pipeline that has never said no has not been tested. The branch-protection point is added: a failing check only blocks a merge if it is configured as REQUIRED.
beats.authoring_note: Run number and version pins are illustrative of a real dependency-conflict failure, not a captured log.

beats.narration_text: And now the uncomfortable part. C.I. would not have caught the bug I opened this video with. A test that calls fire_webhook and checks that it did not raise an exception passes perfectly against a function that only prints. The pipeline would be green, the merge would be allowed, and the alert would still never arrive. The only test that catches it is one that asserts the request actually left — that the transport was called, with that U.R.L., carrying that payload. Automation does not add rigour. It repeats whatever rigour you already had.
beats.new_visual_element: Two tests. One of them is furniture.

props.hotNote: passes against a function whose whole body is a print
props.code:
def test_webhook(httpx_mock):
    httpx_mock.add_response(status_code=200)

    fire_webhook(incident)

    req = httpx_mock.get_request()
    assert req is not None
    assert req.url.path == "/webhook/incident"
    assert req.read()["claim_id"] == "claim_042"
props.stampSub: the request left the process, or the test fails

beats.authoring_note: BEAT ADDED, and it is the reel's point. The supplied script treats the pipeline as the fix for the hook's bug; it is not. A test with no assertion about the side effect passes against the broken function, so the pipeline would have shipped it green. Mock-transport assertion is the actual fix.

beats.narration_text: So: never trust your own manual testing, and do not trust a green pipeline either. Trust assertions about effects that left the process. Automate your paranoia — but write the paranoia first.

props.title: .github/workflows/ci.yml
props.code:
on: [push, pull_request]

jobs:
  gauntlet:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - run: pip install -r requirements.txt
      - run: pytest -q

# TASK: automate your paranoia.

# Then mark 'gauntlet' a REQUIRED check —
# otherwise red is just a colour.
props.sparkLine: Let the robots test the robots.

beats.authoring_note: The required-check note is the reel's addition and the same correction made in an earlier week: an unenforced check blocks nothing.

beats.narration_text: Here is the prompt worth running against your own suite. Ask a model to delete the body of one function and tell you which tests still pass. Anything that survives that is decoration. I ran it on mine, and that is how I found out what I had actually been testing.

props.command: Replace the body of this function with `pass`, then tell me which of my tests still pass. For each one, name the side effect it should have asserted and never did.

beats.narration_text: Let the robots test the robots — but check that the robots are asserting something. Onkar Bhujbal, for Humanitarians AI.
